messages.subject: Re: Combining greek symbols and regular text in axis labels
messages.subject_clean: Combining greek symbols and regular text in axis labels
messages.body_plain:
This is a definite FAQ - shows up about once every year (or more -- this is 
mostly a copy of a message from about 3 months ago).  Here are several
solutions (mine and others that have been suggested):

(1) for a single Greek character: use the "symbol" font (Font 13 on Unix
systems, I don't know about the PCs).

(2) if it suits your needs and you are on a PC, use the graph editing
features.

(3) if you need to mix things up in one label, use my "postscriptfonts"
archive from Statlib. THese functions allow you to create simple to
moderately complex labels using a string with escape sequences for change
of font, super and subscripts, change of size, etc.  Takes some fiddling
to make it beautiful but it works entirely within S-plus, so if you have
to re-run the graphic, the labels still come out as you want.  

(4) If you are a LaTeX or TeX user, use the "psfrag" utilities (there are
a few variations around), so you can create the label in those languages
and have them appear within a PostScript plot.  The way to go for truly
high-quality typesetting, but requires some additional steps.

(5) Edit the postscript output in Adobe Illustrator, if you have it or
can obtain it.  You not only can edit the text, you can easily modify the
appearance of fonts, symbols, colors, lines, etc. with great
flexibility.  Or use ghostscript to translate the ps file to Adobe
Illustrator format, and edit the translated file in Mayura Draw
(shareware from www.mayura.com).  But neither approach works well if you
ever make mistakes, as you have to repeat the whole process manually if
you have to regenerate the PostScript file.

SOME OTHER RESPONSES FROM LAST TIME THIS CAME UP:

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. From Mike.Prager at noaa.gov:

I am tempted to label yours a PIQ -- Persistently Ignored Question.  At
least, MathSoft has not responded so far to a chorus of requests for more
flexibility using math and Greek in axis labels.

Several methods are used for this sort of thing, none of them very
desirable, IMO.  I will sketch out what I know of them; I'm sure others,
more knowledgeable than I, will fill in the details.

On Windows, one can use editable graphics, which support limited math
expressions, then capture the commands generated by S-Plus and use them in
future scripts.  I have found this to work well in some cases, but in
others, the graph after exporting to EPS exhibits faulty spacing of the
superscripts.

Several other solutions better suited to Unix have been put forth, mostly
relying on other software, shell scripts, and/or patches to generated
PostScript code.  What they have in common is that they apparently work for
many users, but they seem to be operating-system and configuration
specific.  If you can search the archives of this news group, you will find
one supplied by Greg Snow MathSoft recently, and another approach by Alan
Zaslovsky (whose name I may have spelled wrong).

Finally, R (a free implementation of an S-like language) provides use of
math in figures.  This was not well documented last time I looked (several
months ago), but may be by now, and I don't know if R includes Trellis
graphics or not.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

2. From bje at lif.hi.is

If you are going to import files into LaTeX you should be able
to use psfrags to replace axis labels with LaTeX-style labels.

You will need to declare \usepackage{psfrags} in your preamble.

A helpful URL is

www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~rrw1/Computing/latricks.html

Bjarki Eldon

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

6. From scw at io.harvard.edu Fri Jul 21 16:14:10 2000
Date: Fri, 21 Jul 2000 08:59:56 -0400 (EDT)
From: Steve Wofsy <scw at io.harvard.edu>
Reply-To: Steven_Wofsy at harvard.edu
To: thacker at aoml.noaa.gov
Subject: sups and subs

Carlisle--you can install the attached functions supsub and msupsub,
which work like text and mtext, to get the capability to superscript,
subscript, mix in Greek, mix colors, etc.  There is also LEGND, like
legend(), with similar capabilities.

Let me know if a piece is missing.  This version uses a generic set of
font metrics, so the spacing may have to be adjsuted with blanks.  Since
the font metrics are different in motif() or openlook() vs. postscript,
best do this adjustment using postscript output.

messages.subject: Re: Summary - Jonckheere-Terstra Ordered Alternatives
messages.body_plain:
I wish to thank Tom Filloon (filloon.tg at pg.com) and Luciano Molinari 
(Luciano.Molinari at kispi.unizh.ch) who shared their code for computing the JT 
test for ordered alternatives.  I found Luciano's most useful as the code 
incorporated Lehman's adjustment for ties, and I was easily able to reproduce 
results from Example 2 in Hollander & Wolfe ('Nonparametric Statistical 
Methods, 1973, John Wiley & Sons, pages 120-123), ignoring Lehman's adjustment 
for ties.  Luciano's code is attached. 

                Regards,

James Pratt
SONUS Pharmaceuticals
jimp at sonuspharma.com

jonckheere<-function(y, groups)
{
        if(!is.ordered(groups)){
                groups <- as.factor(groups)
                cat("groups not an ordered factor.\n")
        }
        cat("Ordering Used \n\n")
        cat(paste(levels(groups),collapse=" < "),"\n\n")
        lev <- levels(groups)
        nlev <- length(lev)
        if(nlev < 2) {
                cat("No case for Jonckeree \n")
                return(NULL)
        }
        jonck <- 0
        ties.p <- F
        for(i in 1:(nlev - 1))
                for(j in (i + 1):nlev) {
                        xx <- y[groups == lev[i]]
                        yy <- y[groups == lev[j]]
                        xy <- c(xx, yy)
                        ties.p <- ties.p | (length(xy) !=length(unique(xy)))
                        sss <- length(xx) * length(yy) + (length(xx) *
                                (length(xx) + 1))/2 - 
sum(rank(xy)[1:length(xx)])
                        jonck <- jonck + sss
                }
#for ties see Lehmann p.235ff
        names(jonck) <- NULL
        ns <- tabulate(as.numeric(groups))
        nn <- length(y)
        expj <- (nn * nn - sum(ns * ns))/4
        if(!ties.p) {
                varj <- (nn * nn * (2 * nn + 3) - sum(ns * ns * (2 * ns + 
3)))/72
        }
        else {
                nun <- as.vector(table(y))
                varj <- (nn * (nn - 1) * (2 * nn + 5) - 
                                sum(ns * (ns - 1) * (2 * ns + 5)) - 
                                sum(nun * (nun - 1) * (2 * nun + 5)))/72 + 
                                (sum(ns * (ns - 1) * (ns -      2)) * sum(nun * 
(nun - 1) * 
                                (nun - 2)))/(36 * nn * (nn - 1) * (nn - 2)) + 
                                (sum(ns * (ns - 1)) * sum(nun * (nun - 1)))/(8 
* nn * (nn - 1))
        }
        c(Jonckheere = jonck, ExpJ = expj, VarJ = varj, 
                P = 1 - pnorm((jonck- expj)/sqrt(varj)))
}

#data from H&W, Example 2
#to replicate H&W results, modify jonckeere function to always use var function 
based on no ties
                hwex2<-data.frame(resp=c(40,35,38,43,44,41,38,40,47,
                44,40,42,48,40,45,43,46,44),
                group=ordered(rep(1:3,each=6),levels=1:3,
                        labels=c('No Info.','Rough Info.','Accurate Info.')))

jonckheere(hwex2$resp,hwex2$group)

>>> "Jim Pratt" <JimP at sonuspharma.com> 09/18/2000 01:56:13 PM >>>

I am in need of code to perform a Jonckheere-Terpstra Ordered Alternatives test 
of some continuous data.  I am hoping others may have available code to share.  
Any help would be appreciated.

Thanks,

James Pratt

messages.subject: RE: RE: Where is the max value?
messages.body_plain:
The location of the maximum values of a matrix can be simply done as:

 > cbind(row(y)[y==max(y)], col(y)[y==max(y)])
     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    4    2
[2,]    3    3
[3,]    2    4

For "approximate equality" it's the equality (==) one wants fuzzy.  Defining

"%~=%" <- function(x, y, epsilon = 1e-010)
{
 (abs(x - y)/(abs(x) + epsilon) < epsilon)
}

We can then do:

> 5000000 %~=% 5000000.001
[1] F
> 5000000 %~=% 5000000.0001
[1] T

And hence we can do a fuzzy max:

> cbind(row(y)[y%~=%max(y)], col(y)[y%~=%max(y)])
     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    4    2
[2,]    3    3
[3,]    2    4

or a fuzzy min:

cbind(row(y)[y %~=% min(y)], col(y)[y %~=% min(y)])
     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    1    1
[2,]    2    1
[3,]    3    1
[4,]    4    1
[5,]    1    2
[6,]    2    2
[7,]    1    3
[8,]    1    4
[9,]    4    4

or a fuzzy median, ...

-John Wallace

Scott Chasalow wrote:

> Hi,
>
> I would just add a wee warning, which I believe has graced the pages of this
> mailing list more than once before, about this sort of thing.  Because the
> matrix x often may contain elements resulting from finite-precision
> computations,  using max.val == x might not give you the result you really
> want or expect.  (Do you want to consider 1.0000000000001 to be equal to 1,
> or not?)  To avoid this sort of problem, I wrote a little function I call
> fuzzymax(), which incorporates a test for "approximate equality" (if you
> will indulge me the use of such a term).  I think I probably appropriated
> this test from some code by Doug Bates.
>
> Below, then, is my version of a function to answer Kim's question.
>
> Cheers,
> Scott
>
> ================================
> Scott D. Chasalow
> Cereon Genomics
>
> Email: Scott.Chasalow at cereon.com
> ================================
>
> === BEGIN CUT ===
>
> "wheremax"<-
> function(x, epsilon = 0.0001)
> {
> # DATE WRITTEN:  03 Oct 2000             LAST REVISED:  03 Oct 2000
> # AUTHOR:  Scott D. Chasalow  (Scott.Chasalow at cereon.com)
> #
> # DESCRIPTION:
> #       Finds the row and column indices of elements of a matrix
> #       that are within a specified tolerance from the maximum value
> #       in the matrix.
> #
> # REQUIRED ARGUMENTS:
> # x     a numeric matrix.
> #
> # OPTIONAL ARGUMENTS:
> # epsilon:  a single positive numeric value, controlling the tolerance
> #       for deciding if an element of x is equal to the maximum.  The
> #       default is 0.0001.
> #
> # VALUE:
> #       a numeric matrix with two columns.  Column 1 gives the row
> #       indices and column 2 the column indices of the elements of x
> #       that are within the specified tolerance from max(x).
> #
> # DETAILS:
> #       An element of x is declared equal to max(x) if the absolute
> #       value of the relative difference between the element and
> #       max(x) is less than epsilon.  That is, if
> #       abs(x - max(x))/(abs(max(x) + epsilon) < epsilon.
> #
> # SEE ALSO:
> #       fuzzymax, rowcol
> #
>      d <- dim(x)
>      if(length(d) != 2)
>           stop("x not a matrix.")
>      rowcol(which(fuzzymax(x, epsilon = epsilon)), d[1], d[2])
> }
> "rowcol"<-
> function(pos, nr, nc)
> {
> # DATE WRITTEN:  24 Jun 1998             LAST REVISED:  24 Jun 1998
> # AUTHOR:  Scott D. Chasalow  (Scott.Chasalow at users.pv.wau.nl)
> #
> # DESCRIPTION:
> #       For each element of integer vector pos, compute the row and column
> #       number of the element in a matrix with dimension c(nr, nc) that
> would
> #       be extracted if that element of pos were used to subscript the
> matrix.
> #
> # VALUE:
> #       an integer matrix of dimension c(length(pos), 2). Column 1 gives row
> #       numbers; column 2 gives column numbers.
> #
>      if(any(pos > nr * nc) || any(pos < 1)) stop(
>                "one or more elements in pos out of bounds")
>      cc <- (pos - 1) %/% nr
>      rr <- pos - (nr * cc)
>      cc <- cc + 1
>      cbind(row = rr, column = cc)
> }
> "fuzzymax"<-
> function(x, epsilon = 0.0001)
> {
> # DATE WRITTEN:  08 May 1997             LAST REVISED:  08 May 1997
> # AUTHOR:  Scott Chasalow (Scott.Chasalow at users.pv.wau.nl)
> #
> # DESCRIPTION:
> #       Test the elements of a numeric vector for "fuzzy" equality
> #       to the maximum value in the vector.  Fuzzy equality means
> #       that the absolute value of the relative (percent) difference
> #       between the element and the maximum value is less than a given
> #       threshold. Support for function f2qpos.
> #
> # REQUIRED ARGUMENTS:
> # x:    a numeric vector (e.g. of ploglik values)
> #
> # OPTIONAL ARGUMENTS:
> # epsilon:  a single numeric value, controlling the tolerance for
> #       deciding if an element of x is equal to the maximum
> #
> # VALUE:
> #       a logical vector. The ith element is TRUE if x[i] is equal
> #       (within tolerance) to max(x).
> #
>      xmax <- max(x)
>      epsilon <- epsilon[1]
>      best <- (abs(x - xmax)/(abs(xmax) + epsilon) < epsilon)
>      names(best) <- names(x)
>      best
> }
>
> === END CUT ===
>
> -----Original Message-----
> From: Gregory R. Warnes [mailto:warnes at biostat.washington.edu]
> Sent: Wednesday, 04 October, 2000 15:58
> To: Kim Elmore
> Cc: S-News mail list
> Subject: Re: [S] Where is the max value?
>
> I don't think that there is a built in function that does what you
> want.  I think this function will do what you want:
>
> where.max _ function(x)
> {
>    max.val _ max(x)
>
>    row.mat _ matrix( 1:(dim(x)[1]), nrow=dim(x)[1], ncol=dim(x)[2], byrow=F)
>    col.mat _ matrix( 1:(dim(x)[2]), nrow=dim(x)[1], ncol=dim(x)[2], byrow=T)
>    return( cbind(row=row.mat[max.val==x],col=col.mat[max.val==x]) )
> }
>
> For example:
>
> > y _ matrix(c(1, 1, 1, 1,
> +            1, 1, 2, 3,
> +            1, 2, 3, 2,
> +            1, 3, 2, 1),
> +            nrow = 4, ncol = 4, byrow=TB)
> > y
>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
> [1,]    1    1    1    1
> [2,]    1    1    2    3
> [3,]    1    2    3    2
> [4,]    1    3    2    2
> > where.max(y)
>      row col
> [1,]   4   2
> [2,]   3   3
> [3,]   2   4
> > y[where.max(y)]
> [1] 3 3 3
>
> -Greg
>

>

>   KE>> this before, but I cannot remember how to do it again, and I haven't
>   KE>> stumbled across it yet in the S-Plus help files.  This is

> contains
>   KE>> the max value.  Because I'm working with a symmetric matrix, there

messages.body_plain:
Aaron J Mackey reports:

> 
> So I figured out how to install the MASS library, 

well done...so did I!

> and now am trying to
> work the mixture of two normals problem with some of my own data:
> 
> Version 5.1 Release 1 for DEC alpha, Digital UNIX (OSF/1) V4.0 : 1999 
> 
> > summary(mydata)
>          X          
>     Min.:-0.02650  
>  1st Qu.: 0.03275  
>   Median: 0.07350  
>     Mean: 0.25970  
>  3rd Qu.: 0.16680  
>     Max.: 2.89000  
>     NA's: 1.00000  
> 
> > length(mydata$X)
> [1] 224
> 
> 
> > lmix2 <- deriv3(
> + ~ - log(p*dnorm((x-u1)/s1)/s1 + (1-p)*dnorm((x-u2)/s2)/s2),
> + c("p", "u1, s1", "u2", "s2"),

*******
Look carefully at the double-quote signs in the line above !!!!
*******

> + function(x, p, u1, s1, u2, s2) NULL)
> 
> ## take the mean/var of the first half and the second half of the data
> > p0 <- list(
> + p=0.5,
> + u1=mean(sort(mydata$X)[1:(length(mydata$X)/2)], na.rm=T),
> + s1=var(sort(mydata$X)[1:(length(mydata$X)/2)], na.method="omit"),
> + u2=mean(sort(mydata$X)[(length(mydata$X)/2+1):length(mydata$X)],na.rm=T),
> + 
> s2=var(sort(mydata$X)[(length(mydata$X)/2+1):length(mydata$X)],na.method="omit")
> + )
> > unlist(p0);
>    p         u1           s1         u2          s2 
>  0.5 0.00153699 0.0002986542 0.03447568 0.001015618
> 
> > my.mix2 <- ms(~ lmix2(X[!is.na(X)], p, u1, s1, u2, s2),start=p0,data=mydata)
> Problem in ms( ~ lmix2(X[!is.na(X)], p, u1, s1, u2, ..: expected 1115 (223
> * 5) gradient elements, got 892, while calling subroutine setup_min 
> Use traceback() to see the call stack
> 
> What now?

Indeed.  (I'm never quite sure how to handle these completely global 
questions...)

The only thing you are using from the data frame is the vector you
call X and it has missing values in it.  You could have made things
much easier on yourself by simply extracting this vector and throwing
away the missing values first.

X <- sort(na.omit(mydata$X))

Your code is unnecessarily messy and that matters if you want to read
it yourself later to try to figure out what went wrong.  Here's
another way of setting it out.

hX <- 1:(length(X)/2)
u1 <- mean(X[hX]);    s1 <- var(X[hX])
u2 <- mean(X[-hX]);   s2 <- var(X[-hX])

p0 <- list(p = 0.5, u1 = u1, s1 = s1, u2 = u2, s2 = s2)

lmix2 <- deriv3(
   ~ - log(p*dnorm((x-u1)/s1)/s1 + (1-p)*dnorm((x-u2)/s2)/s2),
        names(p0),  function(x, p, u1, s1, u2, s2) {})

my.mix2 <- ms(~ lmix2(X, p, u1, s1, u2, s2), start = p0, trace = T)

I'm not saying this will work on your data, but I reckon the result
will be different, at least!

messages.subject: Error...please help!
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I've written a program that calculates areas of ROC in stepwise logistic
regressions from a number of bootstrap samples.  It seems to be working ok
when I test the program with same number of bootstrap samples (say
nboot=10), the as I run it with nboot=300, I kept getting the following
error message:

Error in [: No dim attribute for array subset: integer(0)

Can anyone tell me where have I gone wrong?  Thanks a bunch!

Ly Mee

function(xdata, nboot)
{
# xdata= data, nboot = no. of bootstrap samples

 call <- match.call()
 n <- nrow(xdata)
 m <- length(xdata)
 ii <- rep(0, n)
 y0 <- xdata[, "OUTCOME"]
 roc.boot <- rep(0, nboot)
 assign("xdata", xdata, frame = 1)
 apoe.glm <- glm(OUTCOME ~ . , family = binomial, data = xdata)
 apoe.step <- step(apoe.glm, scale = 3, trace = F)
 fit <- predict(apoe.step, xdata, type = "response")
 roc0 <- somers2(fit, y0)["C"]

# bootstrap starts

 for(b in 1:nboot) {
  ii <- sample(1:n, replace = T)
  yboot <- xdata[ii,  ]
  assign("yboot", yboot, frame = 1)
  glm.boot <- glm(OUTCOME ~ . , family = binomial, data = yboot)
  step.boot <- step(glm.boot, scale = 3, trace = F)
  saveii[[b]] <- step.boot
  yboot.not <- xdata[ - ii,  ]
  y.not <- xdata[ - ii, "OUTCOME"]
  yfit.not <- predict(step.boot, yboot.not, type = "response")
  roc.boot[b] <- somers2(yfit.not, y.not)["C"]
 }
 return(nboot, roc0, roc.boot, saveii, call)
}

messages.body_plain:
I didn't look at your program in detail but I suspect one of
the bootstrap samples resulted in non-convergence or singularity.

You are using the somers2 function in the Hmisc library so I'm
curious why you didn't use the validate function in the Design
library which automates this procedure as well as traps fit
failures, as long as you use backward stepdown rather than
forward stepwise variable selection (backward is usually 
preferred over forward anyway).  validate also implements
the correct "optimism" bootstrap for ROC area.  Your bootstrap
algorithm is not the optimal one.  Yours is part of the
.632 bootstrap, but you did not code the entire .632 algorithm.

-Frank

> I didn't look at your program in detail but I suspect one of

Another point: Ly Mee Yu obviously thinks step() works for logistic
regressions despite lots of evidence to the contrary.  (It's based on a
linear approximation that has been known for 20 years to possibly take on
any specified degree of inaccuracy, so it can give grossly misleading
answers.  You need to use stepAIC from library MASS instead.  I think
MathSoft should at least warn users who try to use this that the software
is based on a known unreliable method.)

In case this worries anyone else: step can attempt to drop a variable with
small t value that is in fact very significant, then notice and give up
without reporting that it had a problem and without finding a suitable
model.  I've seen quite a few real examples of grossly misleading answers
on real problems.  You have been warned.

messages.subject: assignments to attach()'ed list in 5.1 FIXED
messages.subject_clean: assignments to attach()'ed list in 5.1 FIXED
messages.body_plain:
A couple of days ago I sent the list a complaint that assignments to an
attached list that worked in Splus 3.4 no longer worked in 5.1.  MathSoft and
this list were, unfortunately, of no help.  By rewriting detach(), however,
I've managed to get my code working again.  

My detach() takes advantage of the fact that assignments made to the working
directory inside of a function are actually made in frame 1, and only get
committed to the database when the top-level function has completed.  I think
I've covered the bases with respect to error situations as well.   

See the code below.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
detach <- function(what = 2, save = F){
  if(exists(".on.detach", where = what)) {
    .Hook = get(".on.detach", where = what)
    if(is(.Hook, "function"))
      .Hook = functionBody(.Hook)
    eval(.Hook, local = F)
  }
  if(is.character(save)){
    if(database.type(what) == "object" && error.level() == 0){
      frame1 <- sys.frame(1)
      theList <- database.object(what)

      ## don't copy objects created as side effects of eval(),
      ## browser(), recover(), etc...
      exclude <- c(".Last.value", ".Random.seed", "last.dump",
                   ".Last.expr", "q", ".Auto.print",
                   ".Options", "stop", "where", "down",
                   "up", "c", "go")
      copyObjs <- setdiff(names(frame1), exclude)

      ## copy remaining objects to the list that is attached at position what
      for(obj in copyObjs)
        theList[[obj]] <-  frame1[[obj]]

      ## detach() and save theList in the working database
      retval <- detach(what, save = F)
          ## use immediate = F to enable backing out changes
      assign(save, theList, where = 1, immediate = F)
      return(retval)
    }
    else 
      dbsave(what, save, TRUE)
  }
  ## else, will save automatically if modified & of suitable type
  .Internal(detach(what), "S_database", T, 1)
}
----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Um. That's just two columns of the S dataset ethanol, I think.

There are at least two discrepancies here.

1) You used all.knots = T in one case and not the other.

2) There are ties in the ethanol data which leads to differences in the
internal and external GCV calculations.  (The internal ones must omit the
replication sum of squares when computing rss, as only the y means are
passed in. Ouch!)

Also, the optimization for spar in the code is known to be unreliable
due to mis-initialization bug.  This affects all the current S-PLUS
versions, but most severely S-PLUS 5.x on Linux, which can go into
an infinite loop or, rarely, give silly answers.  This is fixed in the
S-PLUS 6 betas, and so I can confirm this is not affecting this problem.

I think the third problem is that here the range of good spar values
is vey broad, and it is hard to select one.

I cross-checked with R, which gave values much closer to your manual
search and to GCVPACK, actually a little less than each due to 2).

I've long been puzzled by occasional silly fits from smooth.spline
(normally too rough) and here the automatic choice looks too rough.
I think there is another bug lurking in the code.

That's not the right way to test this.  Dither the points to remove the
ties, but do not remove the points.

> >I think the third problem is that here the range of good

I did not say that the differences in spar are negligble!  Look instead at
GCV as a function of spar: it is very flat over a wide range.  It is more
that there is no well-defined single good solution to this example: there
appear to be two and gcv is flat between them.  Removing the tied data does
change the plausibility of one of the solutions.

That's another problem by the way: the search algorithm used assumes a
unimodal curve (of -gcv vs spar) and local minima do seem to occur.

messages.subject: Re: getting rid of text "Given:" on coplot -- Summary
messages.subject_clean: getting rid of text "Given:" on coplot -- Summary
messages.body_plain:
There is a logic mistake at the end of the coplot function. The most
complete solution was from Bill Dunlop (StatSci). He pointed out that this
can be corrected by changing the following text near line 244 of coplot:

              if(show.given)
                      domtext(paste("Given : ", xlab[2]), 3, 0, 0)
              if(!onegiven)
                      domtext(paste("Given : ", xlab[3]), 4, 0, 90)

to

              if(show.given) {
                      domtext(paste("Given : ", xlab[2]), 3, 0, 0)
                      if(!onegiven)
                              domtext(paste("Given : ", xlab[3]), 4, 0, 90)
              }

Several people wrote and asked me why I bother to use that old coplot
instead of the trellis function xyplot. There are two reasons. One, for
some applications, I prefer the default layout of coplot. The other is that
the source is there in one self-contained function and can be changed by
the user-- much more easily than the trellis functions.

Anne

messages.body_plain:
Rolf Turner wrote:

> What is the syntax for specifying a non-default value of
> epsilon in your fuzzy equality "%~=%"?

> get("%~=%")(45, 45.00000000001, 1e-5)
[1] T

>
> Supplementary question:  Can this epsilon somehow be made
> an argument to options() rather than to the fuzzy equality function itself?

How about a user.options list?

> user.options_list(epsilon=1e-5)
> user.options$epsilon
[1] 1e-005

"%~=%"  <-  function(x, y, epsilon = user.options$epsilon)
{
    (abs(x - y)/(abs(x) + epsilon) < epsilon)
}

[1] T

[1] F

messages.subject: John Chambers Statistical Software Award
messages.body_plain:
John M. Chambers Statistical Software Award
                 Statistical Computing Section
                 American Statistical Association

The Statistical Computing Section of the American Statistical
Association announces the second competition for the John M. Chambers
Statistical Software Award. In 1998 the Association for Computing
Machinery  presented its Software System Award to John Chambers for the
design and development of S.  Dr. Chambers generously donated his award
to the Statistical Computing Section to endow an annual prize for
statistical software written by an undergraduate or graduate student. 
The prize carries with it a cash award of $1000, plus a substantial
allowance for travel to the annual Joint Statistical Meetings in
Atlanta, GA in August 2001 where the award will be presented.

To be eligible, an entrant must have designed and implemented a piece of
statistical software.  The applicant must have begun the development
while a student, and must either currently be a student, or have
completed all requirements for the last degree earned by December 31,
1997.  To apply for the award, entrants must provide the following
materials:

·       A current CV.
·       A letter from a faculty mentor at their academic institution.  The 
        letter should confirm that the software is the work of the student, 
        certify the student status of the entrant when the software began to be 
        developed (and either the  current student status and the date of
        degree completion), and briefly discuss the importance of the software
        to statistical practice.
·       A brief, one to two page description of the software, summarizing
        what it does, how it does it, and why it is an important contribution. 
        If the entrant has continued developing the software after finishing
        their studies, the description should indicate what was developed when
        the entrant was a student and what has been added since.
·       Access to the software by the award committee for their use on inputs
        of their choosing.  Access to the software can consist of an
        executable file, Web-based access, macro code, or other appropriate
        form.  Access should be accompanied by enough information to allow the
        judges to effectively use and evaluate the software.  This information
        can be provided in a variety of ways, including but not limited to a
        user manual (paper or electronic), a paper, a URL, online help to the
        system, and source code.  In particular, the entrant must be prepared
        to provide complete source code for inspection by the committee if
        requested.

The entries will be judged on a variety of dimensions, including the
importance and relevance for statistical practice of the tasks performed
by the software, ease of use, clarity of description, and elegance.
Preference will be given to those entries that are grounded in software
design rather than calculation.  The decision of the award committee is
final.

All application materials must be received by 5:00pm PST, Wednesday,
February 28, 2001 at the address below.  We prefer that electronic text
be submitted in Postscript or PDF.  All materials must be in English. 
The winner will be announced in the spring of 2001.

Information on the competition can also be accessed on the website of
the Statistical Computing Section, including the names and contributions
of previous winners.  A current pointer to the section website is
available from the ASA website at www.amstat.org. Inquiries and
application materials should be emailed or mailed to:

        Santa Monica, CA 90407

messages.subject: Re: using lm
messages.body_plain:
> Date: Wed, 18 Oct 2000 07:55:34 -0700 (PDT)
> From: Dan King <dan_k_10017 at yahoo.com>
> 
> I want to build a model like this:
> 
> Y = a + b*X1 + c*X2 + (d*X2 + e*X3)*X4
> 
> where Y is dependent variable, X1,X2,X3,X4 are
> independent variables. The way I use lm is like this:
> 
> lm(Y~X1+X2+(X2+X3)*X4,data=alldata)
> 
> Does lm() work here? Or should I use glm() for this?
> Did I specify it the right way?

lm and glm work the same way, and not as you want here. `*' has a 
special meaning.  You want

lm(Y ~ X1 + X2 + I(X2*X3) + I(X3*X4), data=alldata)

adding some spaces for clarity.  The I() gives the meaning you expected:
do look up its help.

It's always allowed to try it and see if it gets the right answer:
S-PLUS does not bite!   I suggest you do try both to see what the
difference is.  But to avoid trial-and-error being mainly error, you do
need to read up about model formulae in a good reference.

--

messages.subject_clean: time and memory problems in Splus5.1
messages.body_plain:
Dear All, 

I've just joined this forum.  With apologies if you heard many versions of
this question before.  I have just been upgraded from Splus3.3 running on 
a SPARC LX (4.1.4 SunOS) to Splus5.1 running on SPARC5 (Solaris 2.5.1).  
The short summary of this upgrade is that my work has ground to a halt. 
A simulation involving 500 admittedly complex resamplings ran in just under 
15 hours in Splus3.3, on a SPARC LX.  In Splus5.1, on a SPARC 5 which has 
four times the RAM I had to kill the same simulation after 63 hours.  My 
patience ran out. 

My question is - if there is an Splus5.1 user community out there, what 
platform are running Splus5.1 on, and are you finding it at all usable in 
terms of time and memory consumption?  In particular, have any Splus5.1 
users been successful in running complicated boostrapping problems in real 
time?  By complicated I mean the kind of problem where the statistic to be 
bootstrapped is itself obtained via some non-trivial, custom-programmed 
user-supplied function?   Since I obviously can't work under the above 
conditions, I am looking (among other things) into the option of getting 
better hardware.   But can anyone confirm that getting better hardware will 
at least get the time and memory problems of 5.1 to a tolerable level?  
My work involves a fair amount of resampling methods.  Any Splus5.1 users
out there doing a lot of bootstrapping/permutations/complex iterations?
Have you found any working solutions?  Hardware or otherwise? 

Thank you very much. 

Tanya Wolfson, 
Statistician
HIV Neurobehavioral Research Center
University of California San Diego

P.S. I am doing the obvious things of course - no explicit loops, everything
is done via *apply statements.

messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 18 Oct 2000, Tanya Wolfson wrote:

> 
> Dear All, 
> 
> I've just joined this forum.  With apologies if you heard many versions of
> this question before.  I have just been upgraded from Splus3.3 running on 
> a SPARC LX (4.1.4 SunOS) to Splus5.1 running on SPARC5 (Solaris 2.5.1).  
> The short summary of this upgrade is that my work has ground to a halt. 
> A simulation involving 500 admittedly complex resamplings ran in just under 
> 15 hours in Splus3.3, on a SPARC LX.  In Splus5.1, on a SPARC 5 which has 
> four times the RAM I had to kill the same simulation after 63 hours.  My 
> patience ran out. 
> 
> My question is - if there is an Splus5.1 user community out there, what 
> platform are running Splus5.1 on, and are you finding it at all usable in 
> terms of time and memory consumption?  In particular, have any Splus5.1 
> users been successful in running complicated boostrapping problems in real 
> time?  By complicated I mean the kind of problem where the statistic to be 
> bootstrapped is itself obtained via some non-trivial, custom-programmed 
> user-supplied function?   Since I obviously can't work under the above 
> conditions, I am looking (among other things) into the option of getting 
> better hardware.   But can anyone confirm that getting better hardware will 
> at least get the time and memory problems of 5.1 to a tolerable level?  
> My work involves a fair amount of resampling methods.  Any Splus5.1 users
> out there doing a lot of bootstrapping/permutations/complex iterations?
> Have you found any working solutions?  Hardware or otherwise? 

I think you are blaming the wrong things.  Our students are running big
problems (e.g. MCMC, simultaneous analyses of 50,000 time series and indeed
bootstrapping complex code) on S-PLUS 5.1, mainly on Linux but also on
Solaris 2.7.  As far as I recall a Sparc LX is a very small and old machine
(and 2.5.1 is a rather old OS version), and S-PLUS 5.1 benefits a lot more
than 3.4 from a lot of RAM.  (The machines being used here have a minimum
of 128Mb and most have 512Mb or 1Gb.)  [Yes, I know you had 3.3, but I've
forgotten what that was like as it has been superseded for so long.]

However, my main point is that S-PLUS 5.1 is *not an upgrade*.  It is a
completely new implementation, and what works best under 5.1 differs from
what works best under 3.4.  See V&R's `S Programming' for some comparative
timings on different approaches.  In general though 5.1 is a bit slower
than 3.4 (but the upcoming 6.0 looks likely to reduce that gap) on all but
very large datasets.

> P.S. I am doing the obvious things of course - no explicit loops, everything
> is done via *apply statements.  

That's part of the myth.  On 5.1 loops are often faster and use less memory
than *apply statements, unlike 3.4, and I'm sure my students' code contains
lots of for loops.  Since all you are doing is 500 independent runs,
running them in an outer loop should obviate memory build-up (if your
fitting code is correct).  Indeed, you could run them in 500 separate
sessions, or use For loops to effectively do so. You do need to re-tune
your methods to run on the new system.  Using the bootstrap() function now
provided might be a good start.

--

messages.subject: Summary: Pronunciation of 'Cholesky'
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to all who replied.  The question was how 'Choleski' was to be
pronounced (and, for those who verbalize to themselves as they type, how the
S-plus command 'chol' should be pronounced).

I had heard two pronunciations, 'Koleski' and 'Tsholeski', and wondered what
others had heard.  (By 'Tsh' I mean the sound heard in the English word
'church' or 'cha-cha-cha'.)

Of the seven who ventured a pronunciation, four offered 'Tsholeski' and
three 'Koleski'.  Some had comments:

For 'Tsholeski':

        "That's how I learned it."
        " 'Koleski' is very rare. ...  'Tsholeski' is nearest to what I have
heard." [This may be a disguised suggestion of 'Sholeski.'] 

For 'Koleski':

        "I've always heard Koleski."
        "I've only heard 'Koleski.'  I'm 95% sure that it's correct."

There does not seem to be any standard Anglicization.

The rest of this note draws mostly from a discussion about Cholesky on a
numerical analysis news list in 1990; it can be found on the Web by
searching for 'Cholesky pronunciation'.  There is also, as the help page for
the S-plus command 'chol' mentions, a short biographical note on Cholesky,
which I have not seen, in J. H. Maindonald's Statistical Computation (1984,
Wiley).

The 1990 discussion includes a eulogy of Cholesky by his colleague Benoit,
who saw to it that Cholesky's method was published after Cholesky's death.
The eulogy was translated in 1975 by Richard Cottle for Cholesky's
centennial.  Andre-Louis
Cholesky (spelled with a 'y'), born in France in 1875, was a geodesist in
the French military.  He developed his computational procedure to solve
geodetic problems, among which was, in the words of his eulogy, the "problem
of levelling in Morocco."  He died in battle in 1918.  Benoit published the
computational method in "Bulletin geodesique" in 1924.

The most likely French pronunciation of Cholesky is that heard in 'Chopin'
-- the English 'Sh' sound.  A less likely alternative is the English 'k',
heard in, for example, the French pronunciation of 'cholera.'

There were some statements in the 1990 discussion that the Cholesky family
was probably Polish.  A Polish correspondent stated that the original family
name was 'Cholewski', a family of "good Polish patriots" that had emigrated
to France.  The Polish name would be rendered in English, according to that
correspondent, as 'Holeski', which I take to have the throaty 'h' of
'hannukah' , also spelled in English as 'channukah.'  (A Russian
correspondent offered the spelling 'Kholeski' for this pronunciation.)
There is no record of whether the Cholesky family in France tried to retain
the original pronunciation or adopted the French 'Sh' pronunciation.  (A
French correspondent stated that he had had a student from this family, but
did not give the pronunciation.)

If, on the other hand, the Cholesky family was Russian, there are three
candidate Cyrillic letters that might have been transliterated into French
as 'Ch'.  One is the above-mentioned 'Kh' sound -- of 'hannukah'.  Another
is the 'Sh' sound, which would have fit into French pronunciation quite well
as 'Cholesky' and is found in such French spellings as 'Chostakovich' and
'Chalom Aleichem' (at least in the initial 'ch' in each case).  The third is
the English 'Ch' sound 'Tsh', which, however, is normally rendered in French
as 'Tch', as in 'Tchaikovski' or 'Tchekov.'

In summary:

1.  If you want the most likely French pronunciation, pronounce it
'Sholesky' as in 'Chopin.'

2.  If you want the most likely Polish pronunciation, pronounce it
'Kholesky' as in the initial 'h' in 'hannukah.'  English speakers who
don't want to use the guttural might opt for 'Holesky' or 'Kolesky'.

3.  If you go for the Russian, you have some leeway, not knowing the
Cyrillic spelling of the name.

4.  No matter what you say, many of your hearers will either tune you out or
think you wrong.

5.  If you want to spell it the way Andre-Louis spelled it, spell it with a
'y'.
--------------------------------------------

David Pattison
Social Security Administration
500 E Street SW - 9th Floor
Washington, DC 20254-0001

Phone: 202-358-6240
Fax: 202-358-6192
e-mail: david.h.pattison at ssa.gov

messages.subject: Re: time and memory problems in Splus5.1
messages.subject_clean: time and memory problems in Splus5.1
messages.body_plain:
I agree with Tanya.  Here's an email I just sent to my superiors yesterday:
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
I've been porting some of my production programs to the new version (5.1) of
Splus.  In the course of this, I've found that it is much slower and uses far
more memory than the old version (3.4).  Now it should be noted that 3.4
already had a bad reputation as a memory hog.  5.1 is much worse.

To construct the following table, I ran my current program that produces the
Special Factors Tables in version 3.4 and my ported program that does the same
thing in version 5.1.  Both versions were run in new Splus sessions.  I kept
track of the memory usage for each by running rtop in another window and
scribbling down the numbers as I ran each step of the program.

                Memory Use in MBytes
                          3.4              5.1
    Program Step    resident total    resident total   
    ------------------------------------------------
    load data          11      16         248   271             
    recalc             12      17         285   308          
    print tables       15      20         289   312    
    done               15      20         306   328
    ------------------------------------------------

As you might expect, given the memory usage number above, the 5.1 version also
takes a lot longer to run.  Loading and recalcing takes 20 seconds (wall clock
time) in 3.4 and 75 seconds in 5.1. 

I could learn to live with the reduced speed (why would I want to?), but
not the huge increase in memory usage.  In MRA, we have a large number of
production programs written in Splus, and it is not unusual to have several of
them running at once.  The special factors program is not unusually large:
I have several others (Target Tables, Financial Databook, M2Plus, Seasonal
Review System) that are of similar size or even larger.  The figures above
indicate that if two RA's ran 3 programs between them, or if they ran 2
programs while an economist had a large long-running SAS job going, our main
machine (mrpmx1), which sports a full gigabyte of memory, would be overloaded.
We have 20 people using mrpmx1, and none of them would be able to get much
done until the (slow) programs finished executing.

It is clear to me that the new version of Splus is not ready for prime time.
I propose we complain loudly to MathSoft, and hold off on any further porting
efforts until they clean up their act. 
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In MathSoft's defense, Prof Ripley writes (this is an excerpt):

  B> However, my main point is that S-PLUS 5.1 is *not an upgrade*. It is a
  B> completely new implementation, and what works best under 5.1 differs from
  B> what works best under 3.4. See V&R's `S Programming' for some comparative
  B> timings on different approaches. In general though 5.1 is a bit slower
  B> than 3.4 (but the upcoming 6.0 looks likely to reduce that gap) on all
  B> but very large datasets.
  
and later

  B> You do need to re-tune your methods to run on the new system.

No.  I spent years writing a lot of production code.  I did things the way
MathSoft told me to.  Code that used to work just fine is now either broken,
or it takes much longer to run, or it uses an unacceptable amount of memory.
If 5.1 is not an upgrade, it should not be marketed as one.  It should
not be named S-PLUS.  And if MathSoft has no intention of improving the
backward compatibility, then at the very least they should pledge to support
3.4 forever.  You just cannot tell people to build production systems on a
code base, and then come out with 'upgrades' that break their systems.  It's
not as if Tanya and I were coding in a way that MathSoft explicitly
recommended against.  We were following the guidance that MathSoft gave us in
their documentation.

Jeff

messages.subject: Update on Splus 5.1 memory usage
messages.body_plain:
I found that my rewritten detach() function did not work correctly.  I
attempted to preserve the ability to back out of assignments in case of an
error made after the detach() but before the top-level expression completed.
I thought that version 3.4 had that ability.  At any rate, my attempt resulted
in the list getting assigned to an element of itself recursively.  In other
words, I ended up with lists like:

mylist$a   1
mylist$b   2
mylist$c   3
mylist$mylist$a  1
mylist$mylist$b  2
mylist$mylist$c  3
mylist$mylist$mylist$a 1
  :            :
  :            :

and so on, nested as many times as I had attached and detached the list.  The
result was a list about 50 times as big as it should have been.  

To fix this, I made the assignment of the list in detach() immediate.  This
means that once you call detach(), the list is saved and overwrites anything
else with the same name in the working directory.  You cannot back out of it.
As I said, I thought that you could back out of 3.4's detach(), but on testing
this, I found that if you detached a list in 3.4 and then made an error before
the top level expression completed, the whole session crashed.  So I guess
losing the ability to crash the system that way is no great loss.
(Before you say to yourself "Heh, he screwed things up himself and blamed
MathSoft for the problem", recall that I was forced to rewrite the detach
function myself because MathSoft broke it and showed no interest in fixing it.
See my posts from a few days ago about this.)

So, have we now fixed everything?  Yes and no.  The fixed 5.1 version is 
better, but
still considerably worse than 3.4 was.  Here is an updated table:

                           Memory Use in MBytes
                          3.4          broken 5.1       fixed 5.1
    Program Step    resident total    resident total   resident total
    ------------------------------------------------------------------
    load data          11      16         248   271       20     43      
    recalc             12      17         285   308       21     45   
    print tables       15      20         289   312       23     46
    done               15      20         306   328       23     47
    ------------------------------------------------------------------

While the 3.4 version took 20 seconds of wall clock time to run, the broken
5.1 version took 75 seconds, and the fixed 5.1 version took 48 seconds.  So
while things aren't as dire as I thought they were, 5.1 is still using more
than twice as much time and memory as 3.4 is.

Jeff

messages.subject: Summary: appearance of plotted lines
messages.body_plain:
I received replies to my original posting (pasted below) from David Smith (
dsmith at splus.mathsoft.com) and Brian Ripley (ripley at stats.ox.ac.uk), both
helpful.  Thanks.

The problem with the appearance of the plotted lines is apparently a
"feature" of the Windows tools.  No guarantee this will be fixed for S-PLUS
6.  However, S-PLUS 6 will include a dedicated Windows Metafile device
wmf.graph() which does not exhibit this problem.

Until then, other work arounds are ... either export the graph as EPS
(Encapsulated PostScript) before printing it or use a different graphics
device, e.g., postscript() or pdf.graph() instead of graphsheet().  Note
also that there is a free program, GhostScript, which can convert
PostScript into other formats.

JVA

> should be the preferred graphical presentation.  I also experimented with
> different line weights  from 1/4 to 12.  Similar findings were obseved.
> Plots of these 2 polygons look the same only when the line weights are
> hairline.

-----

7 Nov. 1997 - Jean V. Adams

     I make a lot of line plots in my work and was delighted to see that

There is an asTable function in the NLME 3.x library (see
http://nlme.stat.wisc.edu) that does this for groupedData objects.
You would have to convert your data to groupedData first.

> oldDFis <- groupedData(Score ~ GameNo | University, data = oldDFis)

Grouped Data: Score ~ GameNo | University
   University GameNo Score
1           1      1    80
2           1      2    65
3           1      3    56
4           1      4    90
5           2      1    67
6           2      2    34
7           2      3    65
8           2      4    90
9           3      1    89
10          3      2    70
11          3      3    43
12          3      4    78
> asTable(oldDFis)
   
     1  2  3  4
  3 89 70 43 78
  1 80 65 56 90
  2 67 34 65 90
attr(,"class")
[1] "table"

This table has the levels of the University factor ordered according
to increasing maximum response.  Use order.groups = FALSE in the call
to groupedData to avoid this.

messages.subject: Summary: Time and Memory problems in Splus5.1
messages.subject_clean: Summary: Time and Memory problems in Splus5.1
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to everyone who replied to me:  Chuck Berry, Peter Perkins, 
Steve Wofsy,  Brian Ripley,  Matt Calder, Jeff Hallman.  Thanks a lot - 
I got many useful suggestions. 

Here is my problem/question, in a shortened form: 
>> I have just been upgraded from Splus3.3 running on a SPARC LX (4.1.4 SunOS) 
>> to Splus5.1 running on SPARC5 (Solaris 2.5.1).  A simulation involving 500 
>> admittedly complex resamplings ran in just under 15 hours in Splus3.3, on 
>> a SPARC LX.  In Splus5.1, on a SPARC 5 which has four times the RAM I had 
>> to kill the same simulation after 63 hours. 
>> If there is an Splus5.1 user community out there, what platform are you 
>> running Splus5.1 on, and are you finding it at all usable in terms of time 
>> and memory consumption?  Since I obviously can't work under the above 
>> conditions, I am looking (among other things) into the option of getting 
>> better hardware.   But can anyone confirm that getting better hardware will 
>> at least get the time and memory problems of 5.1 to a tolerable level?  
>> My work involves a fair amount of resampling methods.  Any Splus5.1 users
>> out there doing a lot of bootstrapping/permutations/complex iterations?
>> Have you found any working solutions?  Hardware or otherwise? 

The responses were as follows.  I got several messages that confirmed
my frustration with Splus5.1, along much the same lines.   As far as 
hints, workarounds, and solutions, here they are (I have cut and paste
and modified exerpts from various letters, I hope nobody feels 
misrepresented).  

>> From: "Charles C. Berry" <cberry at tajo.ucsd.edu>
>> 
>> Of course, there is also R. The ease with which one can use debugging
>> tools like gdb has me using R to debug C code that I end up using with
>> Splus, but I vaguely remember that one can use these tools in Splus 5.1.

>> From: Peter Perkins <pperkins at ucsd.edu>
>> 
>> if swapping is your problem, i found that running a smaller number of
>> iterations several times (with a quit between runs, try running from a
>> batch file called repeatedly with a shell script) saved memory over a
>> single big run.  i also know that apply is not the way to go
>> speed-wise.  of course, explicit looping is no good either.  if at all
>> possible, turn apply's into matrix operations -- example:  use
>> rep(1,n)%*%mat instead of apply(mat,2,sum).  since you're under unix,
>> writing C externals might be a simple way to remove apply's too.
>> 
>> you might look at R -- it has fewer bells and whistles function-wise,
>> but is _much_ faster.

>> From: Steve Wofsy <scw at io.harvard.edu>
>> 
>> One thing that the upgrade from 3.3 to 5.1 did was to change the behavior of 
>> matrices with respect to row names.  Formerly row names by default were set
>> to NULL, in 5.1 they became by default "".  In running tapply this accounts
>> for a time difference about 10x.  Not sure about apply(), but it could be 
>> true alos in this case.  The solution is to set 
>> dimnames(your.matrix)[[1]]<-NULL just before running apply/tapply.  
>> If it works once, be sure to set dimnames back to NULL just before using 
>> the matrix.  any change seems to restore the pathological behavior.
>> Also, the problem seems to be worse with lists.  Dunno about data frames, 
>> I usually avoid them.

>> From: Prof Brian D Ripley <ripley at stats.ox.ac.uk>
>> 
>> Our students are running big problems on S-PLUS 5.1, mainly on Linux but 
>> also on Solaris 2.7.  S-PLUS 5.1 benefits a lot more than 3.4 from 
>> a lot of RAM.  (The machines being used here have a minimum of 128Mb and 
>> most have 512Mb or 1Gb.)  
>> 
>> See V&R's `S Programming' for some comparative timings on different 
>> approaches.  
>>
>> On 5.1 loops are often faster and use less memory than *apply statements, 
>> unlike 3.4. lots of for loops.  Since all you are doing is 500 independent 
>> runs, running them in an outer loop should obviate memory build-up (if your
>> fitting code is correct).  Indeed, you could run them in 500 separate
>> sessions, or use For loops to effectively do so. You do need to re-tune
>> your methods to run on the new system.  Using the bootstrap() function now
>> provided might be a good start.
>> 

(In my specific situation, using the built-in bootstrap() did not help. 
What's eating up time and memory in my case is not resampling the data, 
but running the function to obtain the estimate 500 times.  What I was able 
to observe in boostrap(), which prints "Forming replicates 101 to 200", etc, 
was that the memory/time buildup is decidedly not linear. 1 to 100 is almost 
reasonable, and then each next 100 replicates takes up an enormously 
increasing amount of time.  But generally I completely agree that 
cannibalizing already existing Splus functions is the way to go. -Tanya.)

>> From: Matt Calder <calder at phz.com>
>> 
>> Here is a tip that for some reason Mathsoft does not advertise more. In
>> Splus5 you no longer have to avoid loops as long as you follow some 
>> guidelines.  If you have a complicated loop like:
>> 
>>      for (i in 1:n) {
>>         ## Do stuff
>>         ...
>>          ## Do more stuff
>>         ...
>>         ## Wrap up
>>       }
>>
>> you can improve performance considerably by wrapping stuff in a function. For
>> example:
>>
>>      for (i in 1:n) {
>>         (function(a, b, c) {
>>             ## Do stuff
>>             ...
>>             ## Do more stuff
>>             ...
>>             ## Wrap up
>>          })(a = A, b = B, c = C)
>>       }
>> 
>> (Here I have defined an anonymous function inline, one could also define the
>> function outside the loop and call it by name in the loop body). The reason 
>> this works is that memory appears to be freed in Splus5 upon exit from a 
>> function, so this prevents the build-up that used to occur inside for-loops. 

Thanks again, everybody! 

 Tanya Wolfson, 
 Statistician
 HIV Neurobehavioral Research Center
 University of California San Diego

messages.subject: coxph rephrased
messages.body_plain:
perhaps a very simple question: percentiles, times to failure, and conf
intervals from a coxph - perhaps a simple answer... feed back is
appreciated.

splus2000/winNT

I am fitting a stratified cox model with an interaction using the
following code involving censored data and three covariates - jft, jfa
and mxjd, a continuous covariate cut into two factors for
stratification.

attach(juv.work)

cjdens<-factor(cut(mxjd,2))

dsplit.cox<-coxph(Surv(event,cens)~strata(cjdens)+(jft*jfa),method="efron")

summary(dsplit.cox)

detach()

Recognizing that coxph fits a common set of coefficients with
different underlying baseline hazards, i wanted to access at least the
variation in median survival generating the interaction of jft and
jfa.  I have used survfit() and print() to access what may be this
information:

attach(juv.work)

cjdens<-factor(cut(mxjd,2))

fit1<-survfit(Surv(event,cens)~strata(cjdens)+jft+jfa)

print(fit1)

detach()

where "+" in survfit() codes for interactions. 
This print() produces means, se's, medians and confidence intervals of
each covariate combination at each level of the strata- these can be used
(I think) to describe the interactions among jft and jfa shaping the
survival curves with differnt baseline hazards.

any comments?

cheers,

andrew

messages.subject: Appending data with the GUI (summary)
messages.body_plain:
I asked how to use the GUI to append data; answers so far (with appropriate
thanks to the senders) are as follows:

1st prize goes to Peter Geiser, who managed to divine what I omitted from my
original post, namely that I was trying to follow the advice in S-plus Help
to use the

Data --> Restructure --> Append

dialogue. This is wrong: repeat S+ HELP IS WRONG* about appending. Instead,
as Peter points out

>   You need to do...
> 
> Data -> Copy -> Row...
> 
> D2 is the "from" dataset, and you have to specify
> a range of rows, i.e. 1:2. D1 is the "to" dataset and
> you can put <END> to append to the end.
> 
        I can confirm that this does indeed work. 

(*Or at least highly misleading -- would anyone like to explain what  Data
--> Restructure --> Append  is actually for? Its results seem to indicate a
very specialised understanding of the concept "append".)

        The other response so far is from Dennis J. Murphy, who points out
that the coders among us can use

> a <- matrix(c(1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8),nrow=2,byrow=T)
> a
     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,]    1    2    3    4
[2,]    5    6    7    8
> b <- matrix(c(3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24),nrow=2,byrow=T)
> rbind(a,b)

messages.subject: Teaching Undergrads with SPlus
messages.body_plain:
I just returned from the SPlus user's conference in Seattle.  I had hoped 
to meet with a few people who had successfully (or unsuccessfully) taught 
using SPlus as the primary software package.  I found people who had taught 
graduate students, and a few who taught more advanced undergraduates, but 
didn't find anyone who had taught rank beginners (sophomores and juniors) 
in a "service" statistics course.

I'm considering SPlus for a course I'm teaching in Spring 2001.  I don't 
want to teach the students the GUI, but I want it there for the students' 
to have some sort of familiar look and feel to the 400 (or so) Windows 
products we have site licensed.

I'd be interested in hearing from any of you who have attempted this.  What 
experiences did you have?  Would you do it again?  What advice would you 
offer?  What textbooks would you use?  Feel free to post your answers here, 
or email me back channel.  I think a public discussion would be helpful 
since Mathsoft is looking for ways to increase market penetration.  We all 
know that the student market is the obvious place to "hook" new users.

Dr. Marc R. Feldesman

messages.subject: Re: stepwise coxph?
messages.body_plain:
I agree with prof. Ripley that the partial log-likelihood is the 
thing to use, but I'd like to point out that this is the same
as the (full) log-likelihood!

Indeed, the partial likelihood is in fact the full likelihood with
the baseline hazard profiled out, i.e. the full likelihood with
the baseline hazard replaced by the Breslow estimator
(I believe that this point was first made by Breslow in the discussion
to Cox' 1972 paper).  

This is nice, since it demystifies the partial likelihood, and includes
the proportional hazards models in the general likelihood framework
(if you ignore the technical point that the baseline hazard is
non-parametric).

        Florin

        *************************************************
        *                   Second                      *
        *              CALL FOR PAPERS                  *
        *                                               *
        *     The Second Asia-Pacific Conference on     *
        *    Intelligent Agent Technology (IAT-2001)    *

                IAT-2001 will be jointly held with 
               The First Asia-Pacific Conference on 
                    Web Intelligence (WI-2001)
                    ==========================

           IAT-2001 and WI-2001 Joint Keynote Speakers:
   Benjamin Wah (2001 IEEE Computer Society President), University of Illinois
   Edward A. Feigenbaum (Turing Award Winner), Stanford University 

                    IAT-2001 Invited Speakers:
           Toyoaki Nishida (University of Tokyo, Japan)
           Zbigniew W. Ras (University of North Carolina, USA)
           Andrzej Skowron (Warsaw University, Poland)
           Katia Sycara    (Carnegie Mellon University, USA) 

The Asia-Pacific Conference on Intelligent Agent Technology (IAT) is a
high-quality, high-impact biennial agent conference series. The second
meeting in this conference series follows the success of IAT'99 held
in Hong Kong in 1999 (http://www.comp.hkbu.edu.hk/IAT99).  IAT-2001
will primarily focus on

(1) the state-of-the-art in the development of intelligent agents and 
(2) the theoretical and computational foundations of intelligent agent 
    technology. 

The aim of IAT-2001 is to bring together researchers and practitioners
from diverse fields, such as computer science, information technology,
business, education, human factors, systems engineering, and robotics
to

(1) examine the design principles and performance characteristics of 
    various approaches in intelligent agent technology, and 
(2) increase the cross-fertilization of ideas on the development of 
    autonomous agents and multiagent systems among different domains.  

By encouraging idea-sharing and discussions on the underlying logical,
cognitive, physical, and biological foundations as well as the
enabling technologies of intelligent agents, IAT-2001 is expected to
stimulate the future development of new models, new methodologies, and
new tools for building a variety of embodiments of agent-based
systems.

TOPICS
======

The technical issues to be addressed include, but not limited to:

* Applications: 

  - data and knowledge intensive domains (e.g., large databases, 
    Internet, digital libraries, distributed decision making, financial 
    modeling and engineering, business information systems and process   
    automation)

  - software and interface agents (e.g., personal assistant, translator,
    scheduler, information filter, tutor)

  - computational intelligence (e.g., pattern analysis and recognition, 
   imaging, optimization, resource allocation, constraint satisfaction, 
   planning)

  - agents in e-commerce and e-business

  - autonomous agents in science and engineering 
    (e.g. aerospace, survey of the seabed and space)

  - physically embodied systems (e.g., autonomous robots and groups)

  - very-large, complex, integrated intelligent systems

* Computational Architecture and Infrastructure:

  - computational architectures
  - ontology models
  - agent-level and multi-agent-level infrastructure
  - communication languages
  - multi-modal systems and interfaces
  - protocols
  - tools and standards
  - heterogeneity and interoperability
  - scalability

* Learning and Adaptation: 

  - soft-computing in multi-agent systems 
  - uncertainty management in multi-agent systems
  - integrated exploration and exploitation
  - long-term reliability
  - neural networks
  - artificial life
  - behavioral selection
  - coordinating perception, thought, and action
  - behavioral self-organization
  - believable lifelike quality
  - classifier systems 
  - evolution and learning in dynamic environments
  - adaptation and self-adaptation
  - emergent behavior
  - evolutionary computation

* Data and Knowledge Engineering/Communication:

  - information filtering
  - data mining
  - heterogeneous data integration and management
  - human-agent interaction
  - knowledge discovery
  - knowledge sharing
  - knowledge aggregation 
  - reasoning and planning
  - adaptation and evolution of knowledge networks
  - distributed knowledge systems

* Distributed Intelligence: 

  - dynamics of groups and populations
  - swarms
  - population evolution
  - coevolution
  - collective group behavior
  - coordination and cooperation
  - distributed intelligence
  - social integration
  - market-based computing

* Formal Theories of Agents: 

  - formal/computational modeling
  - chaotic and fractal dynamics
  - computational complexity
  - efficiency in distributed systems
  - taxonomy of agent environments
  - classification and characterization of complex behaviors
  - theories of perception, rationality, intention, emotion, 
    coordination, action, and social behaviors

PAPER SUBMISSION & PUBLICATION
==============================

High quality full-length papers in all IAT related areas are
solicited.  Papers exploring new directions are most welcome and will
receive a careful and supportive review.  All submitted papers will be
reviewed on the basis of technical quality, relevance, significance,
and clarity.  Electronic submission is encouraged and preferred.
Please send LaTex (MS-Words, or PDF) and PostScript versions of your
paper, and an ASCII version of the cover page (in separate email), by
March 20, 2001 to:

         iat01 at maebashi-it.ac.jp

Four (4) hardcopies of the paper by regular mail are also requested 
if electronic submission is not possible.
Please send hardcopies of your paper by March 20, 2001 to:

        Prof. Ning Zhong (IAT-2001)

        Japan

        E-mail: zhong at maebashi-it.ac.jp

The ASCII version of a cover page must include author(s) full address,
email, paper title and a 200 word abstract, and up to 5 keywords.

Accepted papers are expected to be published in the conference
proceedings by World Scientific, An International Publisher, as a
hardcover book. A selected number of IAT-2001 accepted papers will be
expanded and revised for inclusion in ``Knowledge and Information
Systems: An International Journal'' by Springer-Verlag and in
"International Journal of Pattern Recognition and Artificial
Intelligence" by World Scientific. IAT best paper award will be
conferred on the author(s) of the best papers at the conference.

All manuscripts must be formatted using the World Scientific's style
files for proceedings. The style files can be found at:
http://www.wspc.com/others/style_files/proceedings/proceedings_style_files.html
-- use the style files appropriate to a page size of 8.5"x6".

DEMO SESSION
============

IAT-2001 also welcomes submissions of research projects, research
prototypes, experimental systems, and commercial products
for demonstrations at the conference. Each submission should include a
title page containing a title, a 200-300 word abstract, a list of
keywords, the names, mailing addresses, and Email addresses of the
presenters, and a two-page description of the demo system. Submissions
should reach the IAT-2001 Demo Chair:

       Verity Inc.

by July 2, 2001

Authors of accepted IAT-2001 papers will be invited to demonstrate
their systems at the conference.

It is understood that once a submission is selected for demonstration 
at the conference, the presenter(s) of the demo will be responsible for 
bringing necessary software/hardware equipment.

messages.body_plain:
Hello together,
I know that there is no definitely 'right' way of the  selection of
predictors in regression models, but one small question:

I fitted a logistic regression model and selected predictors with
fastbw(). I tested the interactions with resulting main effects and
finally got a model. The variable we are most interested in did not emerge
as a 'significant' predictor, however, when I included it to the final
model it turned out to be significant (in interaction with another
variable).
I tested the two models with lrtest() and the result suggests, that the
model without the variables we are interested in fits better, i.e. this
variable does not add a lot to the model.

Now the question: how would I interpret such a result? A predictor turns
out to be significant (in interaction with another, main effect
included), but does not add very much to the model?! 

I know this sounds like fishing for significant effects here, and I have
the feeling that it is not worth to report such an effect, but I do not
know exactly. Or should I include the variable I am interested in as a
variable that will not be removed by the stepwise procedure?

The main purpose is the detection of any effect that might be in the data
here, since the sample is not representative there is no application
planned for prediction.  

Thanks for any comments!!!!!!

Matthias

messages.subject_clean: SUMMARY: mixed effect models for binary data
messages.body_plain:
Well, it seems as if quite a few people want to know the answer, so here is
a summary. It seems as if this has come up before - so the archives are
worth a browse. Here is a summary of the 4 responses and other things I've
found:

The bottom line seems to be that this is something that is not done easily
in S (yet - anybody working on it?) and Some Alternative Software is
required. It also seems that once you get to non-linear models with binary
responses that the approximations needed to fit the models start to become
questionable and care is needed (at least).

Here are the alternatives...

Genstat (GLMM) - generalised linear mixed models

SAS can handle mixed binary models. For version 6.12 there is
a macro called GLIMMIX (generalized linear mixed models) and another macro
that is called NLINMIX (nonlinear mixed models) that does nonlinear
fitting.PROC NLMIXED in SAS version 8, 

HLM (use Laplace option)

MIXOR which is available for free from Don Hedeker's website:
www.uic.edu/~hedeker

nMLWIN: see http://www.ioe.ac.uk/mlwin/

The Multilevel site and list at  http://www.ioe.ac.uk/multilevel/ is a
useful place to look, and includes more software options.

There is also some discussion in the S-archives about the use of GEE
approaches, which in my context I summarise as "don't". Your opinions may
differ!

Cheers,

Steve

messages.subject: Line Type in panel.superpose
messages.body_plain:
S-PLUSers,

I am curious if the following behavior in the panel.superpose trellis
function would be considered a bug (Version 5.1 Release 1 for Sun SPARC,
SunOS 5.5 : 1999).

I asked my students to make an xyplot where each subject is represented
by different plotting symbols and their symbols are connected by lines
of different types.  They discovered the following behavior.  As an
example, take the data set Orthodont that comes with S-PLUS.  The plot I
want is

xyplot(distance ~ age | sex, data = Orthodont, groups = Subject,
       panel = panel.superpose, type = "b")

with different plotting symbols and line types, so we do the following:

superpose.symbol <- trellis.par.get("superpose.symbol")
superpose.symbol$pch <- 1:7  # use different plotting symbols
trellis.par.set("superpose.symbol",superpose.symbol)

superpose.line <- trellis.par.get("superpose.line")    
superpose.line$lty <- 1:7  # use different line types
trellis.par.set("superpose.line",superpose.line)                                
     

Now the plot has different plotting symbols, but the lines are still all
solid:

xyplot(distance ~ age | sex, data = Orthodont, groups = Subject,
       panel = panel.superpose, type = "b")

If we use type = "l", the different line types are drawn, but without
the symbols of course.  Now an easy work-around is to write a panel
function that uses both type = "p" and type = "l":

xyplot(distance ~ age | sex, data = Orthodont, groups = Subject,
       panel = function(x, y, ...) {
          panel.superpose(x, y, type = "p", ...)
          panel.superpose(x, y, type = "l", ...)
       }
       )

But this should not be necessary since that is why type = "b" is there
in the first place!

Am I missing something here?

messages.subject: Re: New digest format
messages.body_plain:
Trevor,

It is possible to get a plain text version of the digest instead of the
MIME version.  Just send a message to

   mj2 at lists.biostat.wustl.edu

that has in the body something like this:

   set s-news digest-plain YourAddress at Your.Domain

(If your mail comes from the address under which you're subscribed you can
omit the address part, like I've done in the other examples.)  If you have
access to your list password, you can prepend an approve command like
this:

   approve YourListPassword set s-news digest-plain

Or you can use a separate command like this:

   default password YourListPassword
   set s-news digest-plain

If you don't have the password you'll have to "accept" the token that gets
sent back.

messages.subject: A reminder about the Advanced Programming Course with Bill Venables
messages.subject_clean: A reminder about the Advanced Programming Course with Bill Venables
messages.body_plain:
Advanced Programming in S-PLUS

A course with Dr Bill Venables, CSIRO Mathematical & Information Sciences, 14 - 15 November

More information and booking forms are available from our web site at http://www.cmis.csiro.au/S-PLUS

Course Description:

This course is aimed at people using S-PLUS extensively in their day-to-day work, particularly for data analysis and graphics. It does not cover data analysis directly but rather concentrates on the programming issues that typically confront a reasonably advanced S-PLUS user in doing data analysis. The course will use the recently published book "S Programming" by W N Venables and B D Ripley as a fundamental reference.  Course attendees will receive a free copy of this book.

As several versions of the S language are still current, the first day of this two-day course covers general issues relevant to any current S engine.  These are fundamental to the way the S interpreted language works. This will include as a by-product basic programming strategies for making S functions efficient and effective as well as debugging techniques. The second day will continue the discussion on classes and methods in S, and compare and contrast the way these are treated in S3 (the engine driving S-PLUS 3.4 for Unix and S-PLUS 2000 for Windows), and S4 (the engine driving S-PLUS 5.1 for Unix and the forthcoming S-PLUS 6.0 for Windows).

We will also present extensive examples that illustrate important concepts and attempt to show the advantages of the new object orientation system in S4 in particular. We also cover special topics such as dynamic loading of compiled code to some extent. The course will be mainly by way of presentations with discussion and comments.  All software used in the course will be made available to participants.  The software used in the books, including script files, is already available from the MASS internet sites.  Some time will be available for users to discuss ideas with the presenter and other tutors at the keyboard if they wish.

Prerequisites:

The course assumes that attendees already have some experience with programming in S and some strong motivation to deepen their knowledge. A familiarity with Chapters 1-3 of "Modern Applied Statistics with S-PLUS" is probably an adequate theoretical basis, but experience with using S-PLUS is more important.

Presenter:

Bill Venables is a familiar contributor to the S-news mailing list over many years and well-known for his insights on the language and for the clear and effective way he communicates to S-PLUS users. His first book, jointly authored with Professor B D Ripley, "Modern Applied Statistics with S-PLUS" has become known as the bible for S-PLUS users. It was first published in 1994 and is now in its third edition. Their second book, "S Programming", has been eagerly awaited by S-PLUS users all over the world and will form the basic reference for this short course. Bill was a senior lecturer for many years at the University of Adelaide. He has been giving S-PLUS courses in conjunction with CMIS since 1992, as well as courses overseas for MathSoft. Last year he left the University and joined the Environmetrics Group in CMIS, and is currently working on spatial modelling and stock assessment problems in marine and other ecosystem management.

Costs:

$1100 per participant (GST inclusive).  The fee includes lunch, refreshments and course materials.  

Everyone can qualify for a discount!

10% discount  for customers in the CSIRO S-PLUS Annual Maintenance Program

10% discount for bookings of 3 people or more from the same organisation

For example, an S-PLUS customer who is part of the CSIRO Maintenance Program can bring the total cost down to $990 (including GST).  If 3 or more people attend from the same organisation, the price is reduced to $880.

Bookings

For more information ring (02) 9325 3175 or email S+enquiries at cmis.csiro.au

Booking forms are available at http://www.cmis.csiro.au/S-PLUS 

Numbers will be limited, and time is running out, so get your booking in soon!!

messages.subject_clean: Output components from princomp (was Re: (no subject))
messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 25 Oct 2000, Albert Horwath wrote:

> Dear All:
> Can anybody explain me a difference between output parameters "loadings" and 
> "coef" in principal components analysis "princomp"?
> In all the cases I've checked they are identical. What is the necessity to 
> output these two parameters  if they are the same. Are there any cases when 
> they can be different?

The last three lines of princomp are

        ans$coef <- ans$loadings
        class(ans) <- "princomp"
        ans

so they are always identical.  (Reading the code in S is a great way
to understand things.)

I assume this to help the poor users, some of whom come from a world that
confuses principal component analysis and factor analysis and uses the
terminology of the second (such as loadings) for the first.  I do know that
people who have only read the books referenced there on PCA have never
heard of `loadings' in PCA.

Strangely, only `loadings' are documented as part of the output.

BTW, please use a meaningful subject line: it really does help those of us
who get hundreds of emails per week,
