messages.subject: censoring due to deaths in longitudinal data analysis
messages.subject_clean: censoring due to deaths in longitudinal data analysis
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am posting a general statistical question on behalf of a colleague. It would 
wonderful to find that there was an S-plus program designed to address his 
question; however, any insight into the problem would be most welcome. 

My apologies for cross-listings.     -Brett Larive

Hi,

I am a statistician for a clinical trial with up to 6.5 years of follow-up
with a death rate of approximately 15% per year, and a loss-to-follow-up
rate for other reasons of approximately 7% per year. In addition to 
evaluation of mortality, a key objective of the study is to assess the
impact of the randomized treatment interventions on changes in continuous
parameters which are measured at regular intervals while the patient
remains in follow-up. Existing methods for incorporating informative censoring
in mixed effects models appear to be appropriate for dealing with censoring
for causes other than death, but seem problematic for high rates of censoring
due to death itelf. The problem is that most methods involve estimation of
parameters attributed to the full population of patients who started the 
trial. This seems highly artificial when a high percentage of the patients 
are dead by several years into the study. Does anyone have experience with 
methods for longitudinal data which treat censoring by death differently than
other types of censoring?

Thank you very much.

messages.subject: Re: selection of predictors in lrm() or glm()
messages.subject_clean: selection of predictors in lrm() or glm()
messages.body_plain:
Matthias,

Stepwise variable selection is almost always misleading and for
your purposes is especially problematic.  When you have a special
variable to test, I would use subject matter knowledge to decide
on a list of adjustment variables, some of which need to be
allowed to be nonlinearly related to Y.  You adjust for those
variables and get a test for the special variable.  You can also
pre-specify certain interactions that are plausible, involving
the special variable.  Then you can test the combined main and
effect modifier effects involving the special variable.  For example,
if a person's sex is of primary interest, you might test whether
sex is significantly associated with Y for ANY age, controlling for
height.  The test has at least 2 degrees of freedom (sex main effect
+ sex * age interaction effect).  This test is automatic with the
anova method for the Design library which you are using.  -Frank

Matthias Richard wrote:
> 
> Hello together,
> I know that there is no definitely 'right' way of the  selection of
> predictors in regression models, but one small question:
> 
> I fitted a logistic regression model and selected predictors with
> fastbw(). I tested the interactions with resulting main effects and
> finally got a model. The variable we are most interested in did not emerge
> as a 'significant' predictor, however, when I included it to the final
> model it turned out to be significant (in interaction with another
> variable).
> I tested the two models with lrtest() and the result suggests, that the
> model without the variables we are interested in fits better, i.e. this
> variable does not add a lot to the model.
> 
> Now the question: how would I interpret such a result? A predictor turns
> out to be significant (in interaction with another, main effect
> included), but does not add very much to the model?!
> 
> I know this sounds like fishing for significant effects here, and I have
> the feeling that it is not worth to report such an effect, but I do not
> know exactly. Or should I include the variable I am interested in as a
> variable that will not be removed by the stepwise procedure?
> 
> The main purpose is the detection of any effect that might be in the data
> here, since the sample is not representative there is no application
> planned for prediction.
> 
> Thanks for any comments!!!!!!

messages.subject: 2001 Chambers Software Award: CORRECTION
messages.body_plain:
An earlier version of this notice contained a small but significant
error in the eligibility criteria.  The award is open to researchers who
are either currently students or who are within three years of their
last degree.  The revised announcement below is correct.  My apologies
for the confusion.

lg

                 John M. Chambers Statistical Software Award
                 Statistical Computing Section
                 American Statistical Association

The Statistical Computing Section of the American Statistical
Association announces the second competition for the John M. Chambers
Statistical Software Award. In 1998 the Association for Computing
Machinery  presented its Software System Award to John Chambers for the
design and development of S.  Dr. Chambers generously donated his award
to the Statistical Computing Section to endow an annual prize for
statistical software written by an undergraduate or graduate student. 
The prize carries with it a cash award of $1000, plus a substantial
allowance for travel to the annual Joint Statistical Meetings in
Atlanta, GA in August 2001 where the award will be presented.

To be eligible, an entrant must have designed and implemented a piece of
statistical software.  The applicant must have begun the development
while a student, and must either currently be a student, or have
completed all requirements for the last degree earned after January 1,
1998.  To apply for the award, entrants must provide the following
materials:

·       A current CV.
·       A letter from a faculty mentor at their academic institution. 
The 
        letter should confirm that the software is the work of the
student, 
        certify the student status of the entrant when the software
began to be 
        developed (and either the  current student status and the date
of
        degree completion), and briefly discuss the importance of the
software
        to statistical practice.
·       A brief, one to two page description of the software,
summarizing
        what it does, how it does it, and why it is an important
contribution. 
        If the entrant has continued developing the software after
finishing
        their studies, the description should indicate what was
developed when
        the entrant was a student and what has been added since.
·       Access to the software by the award committee for their use on
inputs
        of their choosing.  Access to the software can consist of an
        executable file, Web-based access, macro code, or other
appropriate
        form.  Access should be accompanied by enough information to
allow the
        judges to effectively use and evaluate the software.  This
information
        can be provided in a variety of ways, including but not limited
to a
        user manual (paper or electronic), a paper, a URL, online help
to the
        system, and source code.  In particular, the entrant must be
prepared
        to provide complete source code for inspection by the committee
if
        requested.

The entries will be judged on a variety of dimensions, including the
importance and relevance for statistical practice of the tasks performed
by the software, ease of use, clarity of description, and elegance.
Preference will be given to those entries that are grounded in software
design rather than calculation.  The decision of the award committee is
final.

All application materials must be received by 5:00pm PST, Wednesday,
February 28, 2001 at the address below.  We prefer that electronic text
be submitted in Postscript or PDF.  All materials must be in English. 
The winner will be announced in the spring of 2001.

Information on the competition can also be accessed on the website of
the Statistical Computing Section, including the names and contributions
of previous winners.  A current pointer to the section website is
available from the ASA website at www.amstat.org. Inquiries and
application materials should be emailed or mailed to:

messages.subject: Question about memory usage
messages.body_plain:
Hi Fellow Splus Colleagues,

I've got an Splus problem here I am wondering if some helpful folks have
a good suggestion or two.

Essentially I am running these large scripts that used large datasets
regularly.  If I just source() the main script file, I can see that the
RAM usage on my PC shot up to 200 MB, 300 MB, 400 MB, 500 MB, 600+MB as
the script progresses.  This is because Splus save all of the created
temp files until it is finish running the script.  So what I end up
doing is divide the script into, say, 4 parts, and ran 1/4 of the script
at a time, then the memory usage is more reasonable as the temp files
are not accumulating and eating up RAM to such level.

My question is that is there a function or procedure in Splus that I can
place in the script that would do the equivalent of running the script
in parts to save on the RAM usage?

I know about guiRefreshMemory().  It doesn't save that much memory as
the scripts are mostly computational and not graphical.

TIA!

Regards,
 - Paul

Call for Workshop Proposals
International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML-2001)

The ICML-2001 Organizing Committee invites proposals for
workshops to be held at the Eighteenth International
Conference on Machine Learning (ICML-2001).  ICML-2001
workshops will be held on the first day of the conference,
June 28, at Williams College, the scenic site of all
ICML-2001 events.  Workshop proposals should be submitted as
outlined below.

ICML workshops provide organizers and participants with an
opportunity to focus intensively on a specific topic within
machine learning.  Often, workshops concentrate on an
emerging topic of technical interest (e.g., hierarchical
reinforcement learning), a unique area of application for
machine learning technologies (e.g., machine learning for
genetics), or a community-wide issue that deserves
specialized attention (e.g., machine learning and privacy).

Proposals

Workshop proposals should provide sufficient information to
evaluate the quality and importance of the topic, the goals
of the workshop, and the size of the interested community.
Proposals should identify one or more chairs and several
other individuals willing to serve on an organizing
committee and assist with publicity and reviewing.

Proposals should be 2-4 pages and contain at least the
following information:

  - Description: What will the workshop be about?  Why is
    the topic best addressed in an ICML workshop, as
    opposed to a workshop at another conference or papers
    in an ICML technical session?

  - Goals: What do you expect will come out of the workshop?
    How will the workshop change participants' understanding
    of the area?

  - Format: How will the workshop sessions be scheduled?
    How much time will be used for discussion, panel
    discussions, paper presentations, invited talks, or
    other methods for encouraging communication and
    consensus?  Organizers are encouraged to focus on
    mechanisms other than traditional paper presentations
    and to differentiate themselves clearly from typical
    conference sessions.

  - Publicity: How do you intend to publicize the workshop?
    How will you reach the most interested and appropriate
    participants?

  - Potential participants: Who are potential participants
    in the workshop?

  - Organizers: Please include the name, postal address,
    phone number, e-mail address, and webpage of each chair
    and each member of the organizing committee.  In
    addition, indicate the chairs' background in the
    workshop area.

Important Dates

    Proposals due:                 Dec. 11, 2000
    Notification:                  Dec. 18, 2000
    Publicity material due:        Jan. 15, 2001
    Written materials due:         Mar. 26, 2001
    Notification to participants:  Apr. 09, 2001
    Working notes due:             May. 14, 2001
    Workshop held:                 Jun. 28, 2001

Proposals will be reviewed by the workshop chair and members
of the organizing committee.  Please submit three hard
copies or an electronic copy (plain text or PostScript) to
the workshop chair.  Proposals should be submitted to:

    David Jensen
    Department of Computer Science
    140 Governor's Drive
    University of Massachusetts
    Amherst, MA 01003
    Tel: 413-545-9677
    Fax: 413-545-1249
    jensen at cs.umass.edu

Additional Information

For additional information, see the web site for the
conference:

     http://www.ecn.purdue.edu/icml2001/

which will provide additional details as they become
available. If you have questions about ICML-2001, please
send electronic mail to icml2001 at ecn.purdue.edu.

messages.subject: Re: Question about memory usage
messages.body_plain:
Hi Fellow Splus Colleagues,

I posted the memory issue last week and privately got a lot of helpful
responses from many people.  Many thanks to Lane Bishop, Mike Prager, Greg
Snow, Andy Liaw, (young faithful) Prof Ripley, and Henrik Nielsen for your
suggestions.

Here is a brief summary of the problem and the responses.

Problem posed:

> Essentially I am running these large scripts that used large datasets
> regularly.  If I just source() the main script file, I can see that the
> RAM usage on my PC shot up to 200 MB, 300 MB, 400 MB, 500 MB, 600+MB as
> the script progresses.  ...
> My question is that is there a function or procedure in Splus that I can
> place in the script that would do the equivalent of running the script
> in parts to save on the RAM usage?

Solutions summary:

1. Simply copy/paste the codes from the script to the command window.  This is
the most direct approach and I've found it to work well and adopted this for
now.

2. Run Splus in the batch mode or from DOS-prompt, via something like:

                splus /BATCH infile outfile

I haven't try this out yet as the script still require a human touch here and
there.  But if the script is fully automated, this would be the way to go.

3. There is a command "For" (notice the uppercase F) that's written to work
with intensive computing iterations.

Again, my thanks to all for the helpful suggestions!

Regards,
 - Paul

messages.body_plain:
> From: "Jacob L van Wyk" <jlvw at na.rau.ac.za>
> Date: Tue, 31 Oct 2000 14:07:07 +0200
> 
> Hallo
> Is there an easy way to fit a Gamma distribution to data, where both scale
> and dispersion is unknown?

Well, how easy do you want?  That's a Gamma glm with just a mean term.
If you want mles rather than moment estimators of the dispersion,
that's provided by function gamma.dispersion in library MASS (see the
on-line statistical complements).

Alternatively, the MLE of the mean is the sample mean, which leaves
you just one parameter to estimate, and it would be easy to get
optimize() to do that.

Also worth knowing is that survReg can fit a range of distributions
but gamma is not AFAICS one that is pre-programmed.

messages.body_plain:
SPLUS2000/ WinNT

This query is about how to include an aspect of an experiment in a survival 
object.

The experiment examined the survival of soil mites living in test tubes 
(yes, it is a suitable home...)

The experiment has four factors: rearing conditions (2 levels), food amount 
(2 levels), starvation duration(2 levels) and density (3 levels).  Each 
combination of factor was replicated 2 times in the experiment -i.e. 2 
tubes per treatment combination. I have data on the fate of individuals, 
each day, in each tube - the tube is the level  of interest for us, as all 
individuals in a tube are experiencing the same combination of treatments.

As I understand it, survival analysis examines the fates of individuals, 
and as you might imagine, there are alot of ties in my data: on any given 
day, their might have been more than 50 deaths in a tube (tubes with 
juveniles could have started with up to 2000 individuals) - which is one of 
two tubes in the experiment for a given combination of treatments.

In the end, I'd like a measure of survival probability for each treatment 
combination, and a method to compare them (among the treatments) in a glm 
like fashion...

How do i nest failures within tube (or some equivalent of this) when 
failures are the dependent variable but the tube is the scale of interest? 
- e.g.:

coxph(Surv(fail, censor)~strata(dens)+(rear*delay*fed)

is currently analysing a data set with 4 columns for the factors and a 
column each for failure and censor; the data set includes the fate 
(failure) or censor for each individual.

My only naive thought thus far is to examine each tube independently and 
then perform a glm on some metric - i.e. the half life - from the analysis 
of each tube.

Any feedback would be helpful and appreciated.

messages.subject: GOF
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I would like to do a Kormogolov-Smirnov GOF in Splus for raw data of about
15 observations.
The Ho: Do these data come from a triangular distribution? (2-tailed)
I'm not sure how to do this in Splus. I'm using the windows 4.5 version
and under the Statistics menu triangular distribution is not an option.

Could you please respond directly to me.
Thank you,
Agnes

Here is the code that I used to generated the triangular distribution:
rtrian
function(nn, lower, MODE, upper)
{
        rtrian <- numeric(nn)
        counter <- 1
        while(counter <= nn) {
                L <- MODE - lower
                M <- upper - lower
                u1 <- runif(1, 0, 1)
                u2 <- runif(1, 0, 1)
                if(u1 <= (L/M))
                        xx <- L * (sqrt(u2)) + lower
                else xx <- M - ((M - L) * sqrt(u2)) + lower
                rtrian[counter] <- xx
                counter <- counter + 1
        }
        rtrian
}
